summary: A decimal with one or two decimal places is another name for a fraction with denominator 10 or 100: the same quantity, the same point on the number line (3/10 = 0.3, 27/100 = 0.27). The load-bearing insight is that the PLACE, not just the digits, carries the denominator: the first place after the point counts tenths, the second counts hundredths, so 7 hundredths needs a placeholder zero (0.07), not 0.7. Teach the two forms as interchangeable labels for one amount by tying each decimal to its fraction and to a single point on a line or a shaded grid, so children do not treat 0.3 and 3/10 as different things.
misconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero — writing 7/100 as 0.7 (or reading 0.07 as 7/10), ignoring that the place fixes the denominator.
Treating a decimal and its fraction as different numbers — not seeing 0.3 and 3/10 as the same quantity at the same point.
Reading the digits after the point as an ordinary whole number ('0.27 means twenty-seven') rather than as 27 hundredths.
Mapping the numerator straight after the point regardless of denominator, so 3/10 and 3/100 both become 0.3.
Thinking annexing a zero changes the value (0.3 vs 0.30 seen as different).

activities.title: Shade, name it twice, and pin one point
steps: On a 10×10 hundredths grid, shade 27 of the 100 squares; write the fraction (27/100) and the decimal (0.27) for the exact same picture, side by side in a place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns.
Mark where this amount sits on a 0-to-1 number line; confirm 27/100 and 0.27 land on the same single point.
Now shade just 7 squares. Write the fraction (7/100) and decide the decimal. Predict and then check: does it write as 0.7 or 0.07?
Compare where 0.7 would fall on the number line versus where your 7 shaded squares sit — notice 0.7 lands far past 7 hundredths, exactly at seven tenths.
Toggle between 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 and place each on the number line to confirm all three mark the identical point.
activities.insight: A decimal and its fraction are one number wearing two names; the place after the point fixes the denominator, so the placeholder zero in 0.07 holds the tenths place empty and is not decoration.

activities.title: Predict then reconcile on the number line
steps: Before locating anything, predict: will 0.3 and 3/10 land at the same point on a number line, at different points, or is one bigger — and WHY?
State your reason aloud or in writing, then place 0.3, 3/10 and 0.30 on a marked line.
Observe that all three coincide; explain how this fits (or revises) your prediction.
Answer a challenge: a friend says 3/10 and 3/100 both write as 0.3 — what would you tell them, and what should 3/100 actually be?
activities.insight: Committing to a prediction and its reason surfaces whether a child believes a decimal and a fraction are different kinds of number; reconciling with the shared point corrects it.

activities.title: Reference grid with reveal flaps
steps: Use a static hundredths grid annotated with both notations: tap or lift a flap on a shaded region to reveal 'this shading is 27/100 = 0.27'.
Open a contrasting-pair flap that shows 3/10 = 0.3 beside 3/100 = 0.03, and a 'why the zero in 0.07?' flap.
Consult a number line showing 0.3 = 3/10 sharing one point.
activities.insight: The equivalence of the two notations and the role of the placeholder zero can be seen at a glance as a reference, reinforcing what was built through shading and prediction.

activities.title: Convert, match and locate (check-up)
steps: Write 3/10 and 7/100 as decimals, and write 0.27 as a fraction.
Match a set of fractions to their decimals, including the contrasting pair 3/10 and 3/100.
Choose which value equals 3/10 from options including 0.3 (correct) and 0.03 (tempting but wrong).
Explain in words: is 0.3 the same as 3/10, or different — and how do you know?
activities.insight: Converting each way, locating equivalents, and justifying equivalence confirms whether the place-value meaning is understood or a hollow digit-copying rule is in use.

checkQuestion: Write 3/10 and 7/100 as decimals, and write 0.27 as a fraction. Then tell me: is 0.3 the same as 3/10, or different — and how do you know?
checkAnswer: 3/10 = 0.3; 7/100 = 0.07 (with the placeholder zero); 0.27 = 27/100. 0.3 is the same as 3/10 — both are three tenths, the same quantity at the same point on the number line.
